Based on the retrieved matches, it appears that there is an association between elevated impaired fasting blood glucose (IFG) levels and increased mortality after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) surgery. Specifically, studies suggest that patients with IFG at diagnosis may be at a higher risk of adverse outcomes following CABG.

A study found that even mildly elevated IFG levels at preoperative assessment are associated with an increased risk of death after CABG surgery. Another study found that those with undiagnosed or poorly controlled type 2 diabetes were more likely to experience adverse clinical outcomes despite similar glycemic progression, highlighting the importance of active case detection in identifying patients at high risk.

Furthermore, a study used data from this same dataset to show that even if patients present with type 2 diabetes have lower initial fasting plasma glucose levels, they may still experience fewer adverse outcomes due to their earlier stage of disease. This underscores the importance of early intervention and management of diabetes in reducing the risk of complications after CABG surgery.

It is essential to note that these findings are not without limitations and need further investigation to confirm the associations and determine the optimal approach for managing patients with IFG or type 2 diabetes before undergoing CABG surgery.
